Marcus had been stocking shelves at the grocery store for three weeks when his coworker Devon brought up the diamond ring.

They were in the back room during the afternoon lull, breaking down cardboard boxes for recycling. Devon held up his phone, showing Marcus a photo of a massive stone set in white gold. "My girlfriend's birthday," Devon said. "Two months' salary, they told me at the jeweler. That's the rule, apparently. That's how you know it's real love." Devon sounded impetuous, already convinced, but he was also asking something without quite asking it. He made minimum wage, same as Marcus.

"Two months is a lot," Marcus said. He folded a box carefully at its creases, thinking about the numbers. Two months meant most of Devon's paychecks gone. "What's it actually for? Like, what does a diamond do?"

Devon laughed, but there was a defensive edge in it. "It doesn't do anything. It's beautiful. It's supposed to last forever. It means something."

Marcus didn't argue because he could see the distinction Devon was making and wasn't sure Devon was wrong. He went home that night, though, and thought about it. His older sister had taken a philosophy elective and left her textbooks around. He found something about value and necessity, about how things cost money not because of how much you need them but because of how scarce they are compared to the demand. He read a section twice, the words seeming to move around on the page.

The next Saturday, Marcus was working the register when Mrs. Chen came in with her grandson. They bought a few groceries, nothing much, and when Mrs. Chen got to the water, she bought six bottles instead of her usual two. The boy looked thirsty, worn out from the summer heat. She was being careful with money but bought extra water anyway. Marcus rang it up and didn't think much of it until she mentioned they'd been hiking that morning and had underestimated how much fluid they'd need.

That afternoon, during his break, Marcus found himself online, reading about a stranded hiker who'd been rescued after three days in the desert. The article mentioned that toward the end, the man would have traded anything he owned. His watch, his wallet, his grandmother's ring that he was carrying in his pack. He would have traded all of it for a bottle of water. Marcus stared at that sentence. It seemed to contradict something he'd been thinking, until he realized it might not.

When Devon came in Monday, Marcus caught him before the shift started. "I was thinking about the ring thing," Marcus said. "And I think there might be two different ways to see it that don't actually contradict each other." He explained what he'd been reading, slowly, trying to get the logic right. "Water is cheap because there's so much of it around. Like, if you're dying of thirst, water is worth everything. But most people aren't dying of thirst most of the time, so one more bottle of water isn't worth much to most people in most places. A diamond is expensive because almost nobody has one and everybody wants one, so each individual diamond is worth a lot." He stopped. "The ring isn't worth more than water because it's actually more useful. It's worth more because of how many people want it compared to how few there are."

"I figured, if it survived that long, the wood would have matured or something. Changed. That's supposed to matter with guitars."

Marcus set his cup down on the windowsill. "What if I told you there's a way to check if the wood is actually from 1969?"

Grace sat at the library's corner table with her colored pencils spread across a sheet of kraft paper, sketching the distribution of shadows cast by the afternoon sun through the tall windows. She had volunteered to create visualizations for the school's diversity report, a project that had seemed straightforward until she began arranging the data into charts. The report extolled the admissions office's success: overall, the school had admitted forty-eight percent women and fifty-two percent women from the applicant pool. The numbers looked balanced, fair even, so she'd started with a simple bar chart, thinking it would take an afternoon.

But something about the result bothered her. She set down her pencils and pulled out the spreadsheet on her laptop, scrolling through the departmental breakdowns. The engineering program showed fifty-six percent women admitted compared to forty-four percent of women applicants. The arts program admitted sixty-two percent of women applicants and only forty percent of men. Physics, chemistry, biology all followed similar patterns, each department admitting women at rates equal to or higher than their proportion among applicants. She frowned, moving back to the overall figure. How could each individual program show near parity or favor women while the total reversed itself?

"You look confused," Marcus said, pulling up a chair. He was working on the report too, handling the written components. "Everything okay?"

"The numbers don't match," Grace said, turning her laptop toward him. "Look at every department. Women are doing better or the same. But overall, we supposedly admitted fewer women."

Marcus leaned in, studying the data. "Maybe the data's wrong."

"I checked it three times." She moved through the spreadsheet again, pointing at each line. "Engineering, forty-eight applicants total, twenty-seven women. They took fourteen of the women. Arts, ninety-two applicants, sixty-five women, took forty of them. Biology, fifty-eight applicants, thirty-four women, took twenty-one. Every single one." She sat back. "This shouldn't be possible."

"What if more women applied to the harder programs?" Marcus suggested. "The ones that reject everyone."

Grace opened another sheet. Applied engineering: one hundred fifty applicants, fifty-four women. Applied mathematics: one hundred eighty applicants, only thirty-one women. The pattern emerged like a photograph developing. Women had concentrated their applications in the programs with the most selective admissions, the ones where nearly everyone, regardless of gender, was turned away. Men had scattered across programs that accepted broader cohorts. The math was suddenly legible: within each program, the admissions office had treated applicants equitably, yet the uneven distribution of applications created an aggregate effect that made the entire system appear skewed.

"So the office isn't doing anything wrong," Marcus said slowly.

"That's not what this shows," Grace replied, picking up a pencil again. She began sketching two side by side visualizations, one showing the raw overall percentages and the other breaking them down by program. "It shows that when you look at the whole thing together, you get one story. When you look at the pieces, you get another. Both are true. They're just not the same truth."

She shaded in the differences between her sketches, the visual contrast making the contradiction clear without resolving it. The admissions office could point to their departmental numbers with genuine pride. The overall statistics were still accurate. What she was creating wasn't proof of bias or proof of fairness, only a map of how the same data could tell different stories depending on how you arranged it. She understood now why the project had felt incomplete. The pragmatism of a conciliatory visualization wouldn't actually settle anything; it would only show the question itself more clearly.

"Are you going to tell them?" Marcus asked.

Grace looked at her sketches, then at him. "I'm going to show them this. What they do with it is something else."

He sat on the curb with his phone—a flat rectangle that fit in his pocket and cost less than a textbook—and scrolled through pictures of his elementary school best friend who had moved to Portland and now made sourdough bread. The morning was already turgid with August heat, the kind that made the asphalt shimmer.

His new guidance counselor had assigned him to first period Advanced History with Mr. Reeves, a teacher who looked like he had been designed in a lab to frustrate seventeen-year-olds. On the syllabus, which Parker had printed out like a child, Mr. Reeves had written a single sentence: "You will learn to think like historians, not like people absorbing content." Parker had no idea what this meant, but it sounded ominous.

When he walked into the classroom, maybe fifteen other students were already there, and Mr. Reeves was writing on the whiteboard in letters so large and careless that they looked like a revisionist biography of the alphabet. The teacher turned around and told everyone to pair up and take a seat. Parker found himself next to a girl named Sasha who had the expression of someone who had already decided this year would be disappointing but was willing to be surprised.

"First assignment," Mr. Reeves announced, holding up two objects: an old brick of a phone with a stubby antenna and a photograph. "This is a Motorola prototype from 1973. The first mobile phone call was made on this exact model, which weighed about 1.1 kilograms. Ten years later, consumer versions sold for nearly 4,000 dollars." He set the photo down and tapped the ancient phone. "I want you to imagine buying this. Not wanting it. Buying it. You have maybe five minutes with your partner."

Sasha looked at Parker. Parker looked at the phone.

"Like, who would pay that much for a phone?" Sasha said, which seemed like an obvious observation, and Parker almost said so, but then he thought about his own phone, which did everything except make him breakfast, and he realized that saying "who would pay that much" was exactly the kind of thinking Mr. Reeves probably wanted them to litigate. So instead he said, "What did it even do besides call people?"

"Make calls," Sasha said flatly. Then her eyes changed. "Oh. Wait. Just calls? No texting, no apps, no internet, you just like, called someone?"

"And they had to be near a phone to answer," Parker added, warming to this. "Or you just got a busy signal, I guess. You had to know where someone was going to be."

Sasha leaned back in her chair. "That's actually insane. Like, how did anyone coordinate anything? How did you say 'meet me at the mall' if you couldn't text them five minutes before you showed up?"

Parker thought about this—really thought about it, the way his brain felt when he was reading a book that mattered. He thought about his grandmother talking about planning dates a week in advance because there was no way to change plans. He thought about the weight of it: 1.1 kilograms in your pocket, just to maybe reach someone. And the price, nearly 4,000 dollars, which meant only certain people had it, which meant something about power and access that felt different when he thought about it that way instead of just dismissing it as expensive.

"I think," Parker said slowly, "that maybe it wasn't actually the phone that people were paying for. I think they were paying for... like, the ability to be reached. Or to reach out from anywhere." He paused. "But that's kind of weird, because now everyone can do that and we all hate it."

Sasha grinned. "Yeah, now it's just torture. You can always be found."

Xavier rolled his chair over and leaned in. On his screen was a simple program that worked, clean lines of Python that did exactly what it was supposed to do. Madison had written nearly the same thing, but hers was breaking. She pointed to her loop. "I start at zero, go to ten."

She scrolled up. Ten. She had ten readings. So zero through nine. Her face warmed. "Oh."

The problem wasn't the concept. The problem was precision. Code did exactly what you told it to do, which meant if you were sloppy about what you wanted, it would be sloppy back at you.

That night, Madison found herself researching the history of the web instead of sleeping. She had seen something in the bootcamp materials about Tim Berners-Lee, but it was just a name attached to an image of a bearded man from the nineties. She wanted to know what he had actually built. The first web page went online in 1991 at CERN, she read, and Berners-Lee had invented the underlying technology. She kept scrolling.

In 1993, he had persuaded the lab to release the technology royalty-free.

Madison reread the sentence. The underlying technology. Everything. Released for free. She tried to imagine what that meant in reverse, tried to picture a world where the web belonged to CERN, where someone paid a fee to use HTML or make a website. The internet would be different. It might not exist the way it did. She thought about all the free websites she used, the ones that had shaped what she could access and learn and know, all of it built on infrastructure that could have been locked behind a paywall.

"So basically he gave away his company," said Keisha, who was eating a brownie and thinking about something. "That's wild."

"He could have kept it," Madison said. "He could have made an annuity off it. Royalties forever."

"Would the web even exist like this if he hadn't?" Keisha asked.

"No," Xavier said. He was looking at the brownies. "It would be owned by one company. It would be expensive and restricted."

Madison thought about the calculator program, about how the bootcamp had cost her thirty-five hundred dollars, and how in three months she would have skills that people paid six figures for. She thought about how those skills existed because someone had decided not to aggrandize his control over them, had instead let them loose into the world. She had stumbled into this timeline where code was learnable, where bootcamps existed, where an eighteen-year-old without a degree could sit in a warehouse and actually become employable.

"But he didn't keep it," she said quietly.

Keisha bit into another brownie. "Makes you think about what you do with stuff you build, I guess. Whether you're building to own it or build to let it go."

Madison went back to her desk and opened her laptop. Her assignment was to write a program that converted currency, another small useless thing, but it would work. She put her fingers on the keyboard and began to think about what she wanted it to do.

It was midnight, and everyone else had left hours ago, but she couldn't let it go. The program was supposed to analyze her friends' social media activity, a project she had pitched to her Computer Science teacher because it seemed simple enough: pull data, sort it, visualize patterns. Instead, the code kept breaking in ways that made her feel like she was trying to read a language that refused translation.

She had decided to historicize her approach, breaking the problem into pieces like an archaeologist working backward through layers. First, she had written the basic function to connect to the API. That worked. Then she added the loop to collect follower counts and interaction data. That worked too. But when she tried to correlate follower numbers with actual communication frequency, the whole thing collapsed into incomprehensible errors. The logic seemed sound in her head. On screen, it was chaos.

Her phone buzzed. A text from her best friend Marcus: "Still up?" She didn't answer. Instead, she pulled up her own social media feeds and began scrolling through her own account as a test case. She had 847 followers. She opened her messages and started counting people she had actually had a real conversation with in the past month. The number came out to fourteen. She tried another angle: who would she actually call if she needed help moving? Six people, maybe seven if she was being generous. Her followers and her real relationships were in completely different categories, kept in separate boxes.

She started investigating other accounts, beginning with the school's popular kids. One girl named Sophia had 2,341 followers. Natalie opened her public messages and found them full of people trying to catch her attention, making jokes, asking for advice, tagging her in photos. But when Natalie looked at Sophia's actual activity—her genuine back-and-forth exchanges—there was a sullen quality to it, as though Sophia was performing closeness rather than experiencing it. Three people seemed to occupy most of her actual conversation time. Everyone else was audience.

Natalie's hands moved across the keyboard almost without thinking. Instead of trying to make her data correlate something that couldn't correlate, what if she just tried to show the gap itself? She wrote a new program, a simple one, that would display two numbers for each account: followers listed, and then a count of people who had exchanged messages more than once in thirty days. She ran it on a dozen accounts, including her own. The patterns emerged like a photograph developing in chemical solution.

The results were stark and strange. Her older brother, a software engineer working for a tech company, had often joked about his acolytes online, people who followed his advice and reposted his content. He had thousands of them. But when Natalie ran her program, his actual conversation network was smaller than hers. The gap between his audience and his real relationships was enormous.

She sat back in the chair, the realization settling into her like something heavy. The program worked now, and it was showing her something true. But she wasn't sure what to do with the truth. The gap wasn't a failure in her code. It was real. People could be deeply seen by a few while being seen by thousands, and those two kinds of seeing were not the same thing at all.
